#1528. Newcastle scrape past Millwall to extend Jaissle’s unbeaten start

Joe Willock’s deft finish ensured Newcastle United survived a tough test against Millwall to keep their excellent run in the Carabao Cup intact.

This competition had been fruitful for Newcastle under former manager Eddie Howe and although this match was hard work – as well as hard to watch at times – his successor Matthias Jaissle guided them through a difficult trip to south-east London.

He called it “job done,” and that was pretty much all it was. “We needed patience on one hand, but also to be passionate and tough. We had the chance [to score] and took it,” he said.

Newcastle have reached the semi-finals of this competition three times in the last four years, but struggled to get any sort of tempo going against their Championship opponents.

You could argue the winning goal came against the run of play late in the second half, moments after Millwall substitute Taïryk Arconte had smashed a low shot against the post.

"Livramento had a NIGHTMARE, he's so lucky" 😨Millwall were INCHES away from taking the lead against Newcastle 🤏 pic.twitter.com/X26aiTL432

Given they were missing 13 players because of injury, this was a brave display from Alex Neil’s side. They frustrated Newcastle for more than an hour, nullifying their attack, to the point where Jaissle’s team looked as though they had run out of ideas.

That was until Lewis Hall combined with Matias Fernandez-Pardo down the left and his drilled cross found Willock who cleverly used the angle to pass the ball into the net. Willock has been rejuvenated under Jaissle. He looked certain to be sold this summer but is now starting regularly under a new manager in the number 10 role his system demands. It has been a nice redemption arc for the former Arsenal academy graduate.

Moments after Millwall hit the post, Joe Willock strikes to put Newcastle in front! ⚽️ pic.twitter.com/rSB8yV6NRO

The victory is all that matters and extends Jaissle’s unbeaten start to five games. Given he arrived just three weeks before the start of the season, that deserves praise even if it is obvious there is a lot of work to be done to improve their offensive play.

Playing in their lilac, or should that be Parma-violet, third kit for the first time, Newcastle looked off colour in the first half. Even though Jaissle named a strong team packed with experience of English cup ties, they struggled to overpower Millwall.

There were a few half-chances as Willock forced a save and Jacob Murphy fired over. There was a header missed from a corner by Sven Botman, which should have hit the target and Yoane Wissa also mistimed his jump after finding space for another header.

Millwall’s two centre-backs, Jake Cooper and Caleb Taylor were immense, flinging themselves in the way of every shot and clearing every loose ball that came into their vicinity. Given their injuries, this was a performance full of fight and defiance from the home side.

However, there was also an absence of quality in the final third from Newcastle, the same lack of cohesion and incision that was apparent at home to Bournemouth last weekend and in the first half away at Tottenham Hotspur.

It meant Millwall were happy to play for set-pieces close to the Newcastle box and Taylor got in front of his marker, flashing a header wide of the post.

That lacklustre first half meant Jaissle’s side had mustered just five shots on target in five halves of football since the 3-2 win over West Bromwich Albion in the previous round of the Carabao Cup.

Millwall started the second period like a side sensing Newcastle were vulnerable. A thunderbolt from Jenson Metcalfe, after the visitors had struggled to clear two crosses, almost gave them a spectacular lead.

Newcastle saw lots of the ball. Millwall were happy enough to let them have it given how little they were hurting them.

So much of Newcastle’s play was slow and cumbersome. Their set-piece delivery was also largely inept.

Neil’s side retained a threat and came so close to taking the lead when, not for the first time, a long ball forward caught the Newcastle defence out of shape and Tino Livramento’s mistake allowed Arconte to run clear and hit the post from a tight angle.

Well in, @Joewillock! 💪 pic.twitter.com/5a8G7lzD3H

Speaking after the game, Millwall manager Alex Neil said: “I’m very proud, I don’t think we deserved to lose that game.

“We had some good moments, and we got done by a bit of sucker punch at the end. But I’m very proud of the lads.”

As for their injury problems, he added: “I didn’t bring the teenagers on as a token gesture, I need to keep the first-team players fit. We’re really at bare bones.

But we beat Bolton at the weekend, got a couple of defeats before that but we started the season really well and once we get everybody back, we’ll be in good shape.”

With the first of the 16 teams through tonight, the draw won’t take place until most of the teams have played next week.

The draw will be shown on Sky Sports on Wednesday 16th Sept, after Manchester United play Brighton. Man City vs Norwich will be the only game outstanding then.

The third round had to be spread over two weeks as the nine Premier League sides in UEFA competitions entered the tournament in this round, as the same time as their Champions League and Europa League fixtures began. To avoid clubs facing clashes, the EFL split the fixtures across the two gameweeks.

Still got some more post-match to come for you, but we’ve got scores from all our matches tonight now:

From the Champions League, Man City held out against Porto to win 2-0.

“I think we had a lot of chances in the first half, and we went in a half-time saying we need to  take our chances, so I’m glad we came out in the second half and we did,” said Willock after the match.

“100% [the competition is important], we’ve won it before so it’s very important to us, but every game is important to us. Especially with a new coach and a lot of new players, we wanted to start the new season well. I think we started really well and we need to continue and this was a big game in keeping that momentum.”

"We said at half-time we NEED to take our chances"Lewis Hall and Joe Willock react to Newcastle's win over Millwall 🎙️ pic.twitter.com/NDF3laD8nT

Take a look at the match-winner from Joe Willock:

Moments after Millwall hit the post, Joe Willock strikes to put Newcastle in front! ⚽️ pic.twitter.com/rSB8yV6NRO

The goal came minutes after Millwall were inches away from taking the lead themselves, as Arconte was denied by the post:

"Livramento had a NIGHTMARE, he's so lucky" 😨Millwall were INCHES away from taking the lead against Newcastle 🤏 pic.twitter.com/X26aiTL432

We’ll be bringing you more from the post-match now.

Joe Willock has done enough for Newcastle to reach the fourth round and keep the travelling fans singing all the way back to the North-East.

It won’t go down in history as the greatest Carabao fixture, but Newcastle found a way to keep their momentum going and give Matthias Jaissle a win on his cup debut.

Newcastle aren’t taking any risks as Hornicek sends the ball long, and the players keep looking to send the ball down-field.

Seconds to go now. Marschall sends it long for one last effort, but it is cleared out of the box...

Willock has come off now for Newcastle’s own teenager, Sean Steur. A few more minutes and the man now on the bench with have done enough to send his side through to the next round.

We’re into the final minutes as Millwall are throwing everything at this.

Millwall are not out of this yet, as Neghli comes down the left side, twisting his way into the box past his defender – but having done the hard work, his shot flashes low across goal.

Some more changes, as Ramsey comes off for Newcastle, replaced by Lewis Miley.

A double change for the hosts as Dykes and Kelly come off for Regan Monty and Alfie Massey – the former just 15 years old.

Seconds later, another teenager takes to the pitch for Millwall as Osei-Tutu is replaced by 17-year-old Tristan Parkes.

Newcastle almost have another! From the sublime to the ridiculous, as Willock makes another run, this time down the left, and passes the ball onto the edge of the box where Elanga meets it in space. He lets it run, before taking his shot, but it is straight to Marschall.

Finally Newcastle have their breakthrough! They punish Millwall as Fernandez-Pardo feeds Hall on the left, who cuts inside and slips the ball across goal, finding Willock to redirect the ball to slot it home.

Marschall releases Arconte with a long ball and he turns Livramento to find huge amounts of space on the right side. He races into the box and takes a shot from close range, aiming for his near post, but is denied by the woodwork and the rebound hits the seated Hornicek. The keeper is lucky to not concede an own goal, as the ball bounces up and over his leg.

Issoufou again racing down the right side, before cutting inside and taking a shot with his left foot. Hall, who has been so crucial in the Newcastle attack, throws himself at the shot, and it flies high for Hornicek to collect.

Replays show that González, who Millwall players claimed had handled the ball earlier, leant down to clear with his shoulder.

Issoufou sends a great ball in for Millwall from the right side, but it is cleared by a Newcastle player, accompanied by cries for handball.

The game is opening up now as Newcastle make a run of their own, with Willock creating an opening for Elanga to take the ball to the edge of the box, before Taylor slides in to block his shot.

Millwall could absolutely win this with a smash-and-grab with less than 20 minutes to go. They are pushing for it but are lacking some attacking quality to finish the job.

From six shots they’ve had two on target, compared to Newcastle’s three on target from 20.

Fernandez-Pardo gets his first look at the ball, making a very quick run down across the centre of the field to the left side, but Osei-Tutu stays with him and takes him all the way to the back line before giving up a corner.

Elanga takes the corner, punched away by the keeper but no one goes to finish the job and Newcastle get another corner.

Metcalfe, who had his red card overturned this week, is the first player to go in the book for a mistimed challenge on Ramsey.

Just a reminder that there is no extra time, so if we’re all square after 90 minutes, it’s straight to a penalty shoot-out.

Willock gets the ball on the edge of the area and passes it on a quick turn to Barnes just inside the box, but there was not much on his shot and Marschall collects easily.

Double change now for Newcastle as Wissa and Murphy come off, replaced by Elanga and Fernandez-Pardo as Jaissle looks for pace. Schar is handed the armband.

Free kick for Newcastle, right on the corner of the box. Murphy takes, but it hits the wall 10 feet away, and bounces straight back to him. His cross into the box is headed out, and for all the opportunities Newcastle have created, they are yet to find the breakthrough.

We’ve also had a double change for Millwall as Esse and Lovelace have come off, replaced by Issoufou and Arconte.

What colour would you describe this Newcastle away shirt? They look like the sweets Purple Violet to me. Although would you call it an all Lilac number?

It’s the first time they have worn their third kit. Not sure whether I like it or not.  Shame The Den isn’t a sell out although I’m told tickets were priced at £31 and Millwall have a lot of injuries too.

Newcastle get another corner after a run from Willock. The delivery from Hall creates a good amount of confusion in the box and Marschall isn’t sure whether to stay on his line or come out to punch it away. From within the bodies, Wissa tries to get a shot off from close range but it bounces and the keeper easily collects.

González commits another foul, pulling down Esse, to give Millwall another free kick from 40 yards out.

The ball meets Taylor at the back post, but he meets it in the air and can’t quite direct it either into goal or back into the six-yard box, so it goes out for a Newcastle goal kick.

Another half chance for Millwall as Dykes feeds Kelly on the right side, who runs into the box and gets caught between passing the ball in and taking the shot, with the ball going high over the box.

Another great challenge from Osei-Tutu as Willock makes a run into the box, but is brought down by a well-timed tackle from the right-back.

The corner from Hall is better, but headed out and cleared.

Barnes again with space on the left side and he sends a ball fizzing low across the box to the far post but Neghli is able to lean on Murphy to stop him making contact.

Scramble for Newcastle as the ball is sent by Dykes to Neghli free at the far post, who puts the ball into a very dangerous area just in front of goal and everyone jumps on. Newcastle get to it first, managing to clear it from the goal mouth. It is cleared outside the box and it bounces to unmarked Metcalfe, who takes a thunderous shot, putting his laces through the ball but he is unable to keep it down and it goes over the bar.

Despite Alex Neil’s premonitions, no changes for Millwall at the break.

Right-back change for Newcastle, as Dedic comes off and Tino Livramento comes on.

The earlier kick-offs of the Carabao third round have just started their second periods, but here are the latest scores:

Aston Villa won their opening Champions League fixture 3-2 against Club Brugge, while Man City are still goalless against Porto, which you can follow with our live blog here

And that’s the last action of the half, as just one minute was added on and that was taken up by Newcastle’s corner.

Nothing separates the two sides at the half, thought the visitors have dominated in terms of possession and chances.

Millwall have held fast and will be happy to be finishing the half level. We may see some changes from them after the break.

The game is opening up before half-time, and Newcastle go again with Hall and Barnes. Osei-Tutu does well to wait before going in to block Barnes’s shot and send the ball behind for another Newcastle corner.

The delivery is once again poor, but Schar is pulled down inside the box by Taylor and is furious that nothing was given. There’s no VAR so there’s no review to consider – but looking at replays, Millwall were very lucky to get away with that foul.

Cooper makes a perfect pass down the left sideline, allowing Neghli to find space and forcing Newcastle to clear it away fo a Millwall corner.

The ball in is promising but Hornicek gets to it and punches it away, but the hosts keep the pressure on.

Baggott floats another ball across the box towards the right back post, but Hornicek easily collects the ball as Neghli can’t quite connect.

Newcastle moving the ball well again across midfield and it comes to Schar, who runs into space and gets a low shot away, around 40 yards out. It  takes a slight deflection on its way, going just wide of the post.

González is not having his best night and makes a silly foul against Dykes on the sideline, giving the hosts another set piece. The swinging ball in is not nearly as good as last time, and only reaches the first man, Newcastle’s Ramsey.

Millwall get a free kick, and the delivery is good, allowing Taylor to connect on the header inside the box. He beats Hornicek but the header rolls just wide of the post, to the groans of the home fans.

Hall goes short with the corner and Dedic has lots of time to cross the ball in from the right. It’s headed away but Millwall can’t break on the counter.

That sums up the game pretty well: not much finishing quality from Newcastle but Millwall not creating much from their limited spells of possession.

Newcastle pushing again. Another ball pulled back by Barnes finds Ramsey at the top of the box, and his ball in connects with Wissa. Newcastle’s captain can’t head it in the right direction though and Millwall survive again.

The spell of pressure results in another corner for the visitors – and now we’re getting some pushing in the six-yard box.

I think Millwall have done well. They have limited Newcastle to half chances and the odd set piece threat. They have made things really difficult for the visitors, crowding them out of space on the edge of the area.

When the home side have advanced up the pitch the Newcastle defence has not looked particularly secure.

As we reach the half-hour mark, Newcastle have 10 shots to Millwall’s one, though they sit one apiece on shots on target.

Esse gets caught on his heels as Hall pulls a long ball back on the left, and in the crowd at the top of the box Willock takes a shot, pulling it wide – cheers from the home crowd again.

First piece of good attacking play from Millwall as Neghli and Baggott work on the overlap. Baggott lofts a high ball to the back post, where Dykes gets a foot on it on the volley, but he can’t quite get over it and it’s easily picked up by Hornicek.

Barnes and Ramsey combine again down the left, with the midfielder trying to feed Barnes on his run. The pass has too much on it though, and as it runs out the back it’s met with jeers from the home fans for a goal kick.

Wissa breaks away down the centre of the field, with Barnes on his left, using him as a decoy. Wissa takes the shot though and it is blocked by a sliding defender.

Newcastle hit 20 minutes in with 68 per cent possession but nothing to show yet for their efforts. You feel like it will only be a matter of time though.

Another Newcastle corner, swung in well and Botman comes charging in, beating cooper to a free header. The defender heads it over the bar and holds his head in his hands. The visitors could definitely be a goal up by now.

Hall’s free-kick is met by the first man Metcalfe who heads it away to atone for his foul and Newcastle remain stymied.

Millwall will have expected Newcastle to dominate the ball but they are really pushing for an opener, especially down the left side with Barnes and Hall.

Again, Newcastle coming down the wings, this time on the left. Esse picks the ball up but loses it and Willock picks it up and takes a shot on his right foot with good power but sends it straight at Marschall. The debut keeper parries it away and it’s cleared by a  Millwall header.

Willock comes down the left soon after and is fouled by Metcalfe to get a free kick in a good spot outside the box.

Murphy gets a shot off after Dedic picks up a long ball on the right side and crosses it back towards the middle of the field. Murphy gets on it and takes the shot inside the box off his left foot but it sails over the bar.

González gives the ball away cheaply and Metcalfe picks it up, but unable to move it forward.

Newcastle will need to make sure they don’t get complacent in defence.

Millwall having a spell of possession, the counter-attack looking like their best option but as they move down the right hand side, Lovelace makes a late challenge to get the ball back and fouls Wissa.

Newcastle advancing, with Dedic and Ramsey moving the ball across midfield. Barnes gets the ball on the left of the box, and his ball is in knocked out and Newcastle get the first corner of the game.

Nothing comes of it as it is sent in high and long over the box.

Fair to say both teams are settling, but Millwall try and create a chance with Lovelace, though it’s intercepted. Dykes takes a bit of a knock and is slow to get up.

Here we go in south London, and Millwall get us started.

Just a reminder of the teams starting today:

Starting XI: Filip Marschall; Jordi Osei-Tutu, Caleb Taylor, Jake Cooper, Elkan Baggott; Lyndon Dykes, Jenson Metcalfe; Camiel Neghli, Daniel Kelly, Romain Esse; Zak Lovelace

Substitutes: Regan Monty, Tristan Parkes, Sacha Vieira, George Beaumont, Yanis Issoufou, George Evans, Taïryk Arconte, Alfie Massey, Zak Sturge

Starting XI: Lukás Hornícek; Lewis Hall, Fabian Schär, Amar Dedic, Sven Botman; Jacob Murphy, Nico González; Jacob Ramsey, Harvey Barnes, Joe Willock; Yoane Wissa

Substitutes: Tino Livramento, Anthony Elanga, Malick Thiaw, Nick Pope, Lewis Miley, Bazoumana Touré, Matias Fernandez-Pardo, Aladji Bamba, Sean Steur

The teams are coming out of the tunnel, and both home and away fans in the Den are already in loud voice. Kick off on the way!

"We've tried to find the right balance" ⚖️Matthias Jaissle on his team selection for tonight's match with Millwall ⚫️ pic.twitter.com/kiRRxAgLk8

We’re just a few minutes away from kick off in south London, but Bournemouth have scored the first goal of the third round, with Ryan Christie putting his side ahead against Lincoln.

Alex Neil has not minced his words over his squad’s injury crisis. His team is down 13 players, which the coach says has “definitely forced” his hand in terms of squad rotation.

Playing two matches a week in the “relentless” Championship has turned his squad selection into a “needs must scenario” and he even admitted he “may need to make a couple of changes at half-time depending on how the game goes”

Matthias Jaissle is clearly taking this competition seriously and having started the league well, he is still trying to get the fans onside and create momentum for his team.

At the same time, Telegraph Sport have reported that Ross Wilson, the sporting director, has warned there will have to be more departures in future windows. Having lost Alexander Isak, Anthony Gordon, Sandro Tonali and Bruno Guimarães in 12 months, there will be yet be more upheaval.

You can read Luke Edwards’ full story on that here

The Premier League teams playing in European competitions enter the EFL Cup in this round, with all 16 fixtures being played over five match days. As well as tonight’s games there will be:

Fleetwood Town vs Sheffield United (7.45pm)

*all kick-off at 8pm, unless stated otherwise

Newcastle have named a strong side – probably the strongest they could field when factoring in senior players needing game time – to take on Millwall in the Carabao Cup.

Jacob Ramsey impressed coming off the bench against Bournemouth last weekend and manager Matthias Jaissle refused to sanction winger Jacob Murphy’s transfer to Nottingham Forest late in the window. Both deserve a chance to impress from the start.

Veteran centre back Fabian Schar comes in for Malick Thiaw, but those are the only three changes from the side that drew with Bournemouth.

Jaissle insisted he would take the competition seriously and the teamsheet proves it, but it also raises questions about some of Newcastle’s summer recruitment.

Bazoumana Toure cost £42m but was withdrawn at half time in the win over West Brom in the previous round, which means Harvey Barnes does not get a rest. That’s a lot of money to spend on a winger who has not looked Premier League ready so far.

Aladji Bamba, a £30m signing from Monaco, has not started a game yet and has been an unused substitute since the opening game against Liverpool. He remains on the bench.

Even Sean Steur, who has looked good since his summer move from Ajax, cannot dislodge another more recent arrival in former Manchester City midfielder Nico González.

Having made a total of eight new signings in a much-vaunted summer rebuild, Jaissle only started three of them against Bournemouth and only two start tonight at The Den.

Early days but this was one of the main reasons Eddie Howe quit – he did not think the likes of Toure, Steur and Bamba were ready to play first team football.

The visitors have arrived in south London

We've made it to South East London 👋 pic.twitter.com/nh8Fpa37xT

We’re bringing you the action from the pick of tonight’s EFL Cup games but there are also four games kicking off at 7.45pm:

The Champions League also returns tonight and you can follow along with both our blogs:

Aston Villa are currently 3-1 up against Club Brugge in Belgium – follow the action here

Manchester City will face Porto at 8.00pm – our live blog has just gone live here with the team news from both sides

Yoane Wissa takes the captain’s armband tonight, while Jacob Ramsey starts up front after scoring a late equaliser against Bournemouth on Saturday

Your Mags at Millwall ✊ pic.twitter.com/zfnHgTlWgh

Keeper Filip Marschall is making his debut while Jensen Metcalfe is back in the squad after his red card against Bolton was overturned on appeal

How your Lions line-up tonight 🔢 pic.twitter.com/wEp6qLIz4Y

Welcome to tonight’s live coverage of Millwall vs Newcastle United, as the Geordies travel to south London for the third round of the Carabao Cup.

Newcastle held off West Brom in their second-round match, with Harvey Barnes scoring two second-half goals to see his side through. It was a mighty comeback, after Isaac Price scored early to stun the crowd at St James’ Park. Bazoumana Toure equalised for Matthias Jaissle’s side just before half-time, and Barnes, his replacement in the second half, put them ahead minutes after the restart. West Brom pulled it back to 2-2 with a penalty converted by Price after Lewis Hall was deemed to have handled the ball in the box, but Barnes got his second just nine minutes from full-time and the hosts were able to see out the match to progress.

Alex Neil’s Millwall have reached round three via a 0-1 win over Cambridge United, following a penalty shoot-out in the first round to beat QPR. They come into this tie with a squad stretched thin, as they have been hit with an injury crisis a month into the new season. Millwall have confirmed that they will be without Casper De Norre, Josh Coburn, Tristan Crama, Alfie Doughty, Mathis Servais, Ryan Leonard, Mihailo Ivanovic, Lukas Jensen and Luke Cundle.

Both sides sit seventh in their respective leagues, with Millwall on a record of three wins and two losses this season, while Newcastle remain unbeaten (two draws and a win).

Newcastle will hoping to progress smoothly in a tournament that they have recently enjoyed good form in – winners in 2025 and semi-finalists last season – and with Millwall dealing with a bare bones squad, the Championship side are the underdogs on paper going into this fixture.

But, as always, anything can happen, so let us know your score prediction in the comments and we’ll be bringing you team news soon!

#1527. Mazzara: ‘A core of 16-18 high level players’ – Cardinale hopes to take Milan to new levels

Gerry Cardinale has invested heavily in AC Milan recently and there are no plans to slow down anytime soon.

Since the restructuring of the vendor loan, Cardinale has completely changed his ownership style. More actively involved, the American has seemingly fallen in love with the club and has become desperate to see it succeed.

Read SempreMilan ad-free and get access to exclusive news. Click here for a free trial!

Glimpses were seen before the mercato, with him regularly visiting the training ground. However, his work since then – spending €150 million on transfers and attending every Serie A game so far – shows the level of dedication he has to the cause.

In January, the American is expected to spend heavily, too. A €70 million bid for Endrick is being prepared, whilst he is also determined to sign Goncalo Inacio. It’s clear that he wants to raise the level of the starters and those who will contribute from the bench.

In an editorial for MilanNews today, Pietro Mazzara looked at the current squad and what Cardinale plans to do.

“AC Milan’s transfer market is poised for significant events because Gerry Cardinale has no intention of stopping. His comments in recent days, both public and private, are a clear statement of what the AC Milan owner intends to do to bring AC Milan back to the top.

“Whether he succeeds or not will only be determined by time and the type of decisions he makes, but he certainly has the desire, vision, and financial resources. One can expect anything from someone who beat out Netflix for the Warner Bros. acquisition.

“Among the many things he has learned is that the climate of mediocrity surrounding results has undermined the mentality of a club and an environment that, instead, must strive to always be at the top.

“But returning to those levels requires several factors: a clear decision-making structure (which will be finalised by Markus Krösche, who will always report to Cardinale, who will always have the final say and be involved in negotiations), strong players in the squad, a political presence in the halls of power, a connection with the fans, and credibility.

“What may seem like slogans in themselves are actually manifestos that one can legitimately believe or not. The only way to evaluate Cardinale’s work is to observe how he operates and then draw conclusions.

“He’s fired up, and between January and next summer there will be some serious transfer campaigns. The reason is simple: there’s a need to significantly raise the squad’s level, creating a core of 16-18 players of a certain caliber who can be joined by young players to develop and develop.

“This is why Milan will be looking for not only technically strong players, but also leaders who can complement those already in the Milan core group.

“It’s crucial to raise the team’s personality, including strong personalities who can provide a different kind of motivation during the day-to-day at Milanello. These players, inevitably, cost money, but Cardinale doesn’t want to set limits.

“This doesn’t mean Milan will sign a player worth one hundred million euros, but it does mean they can continue along the operational path laid out by Diego Moreira. All of this is in concert and in line with Ruben Amorim, who is fiercely defended by the AC Milan owner and with whom he intends to begin a long-term relationship.

“And the vision is to acquire the Van Dijks in the pre-prime phase rather than signing them at 35 (assuming, for the sake of argument, that I’d sign someone like that now).

“In my opinion, a Sandro Tonali- style signing is needed. And it’s not out of the question that Milan could try to bring him back in the coming years, even though he currently plays for a club as complex to negotiate with as Tottenham.

“Meanwhile, discussions are ongoing to finalise the renewal of Adrien Rabiot and Alphadjo Cisse.”

#1526. McKennie fit for Fiorentina as Juventus chase a third straight win before the break

Weston McKennie is over the muscle problem that kept him out at AZ and is set to start in Florence on Sunday. A win would send Spalletti's depleted side into the international break on a three-match winning run.

Juventus close the round in Florence with a familiar midfielder back. Spalletti will hand Weston McKennie an immediate return to the side, Sky Sport Italia reports. The return comes at a useful moment for a squad that is still stretched.

#FiorentinaJuve 🔜 https://t.co/ST1eWZieA8

— JuventusFC (@juventusfc) November 6, 2026

Celik and Conceição face late fitness checks and may only make the bench. Before the AZ match, Çelik was one of three Juventus players with at least two goals in this Europa League campaign, alongside Nick Woltemade and Randal Kolo Muani. The club’s squad list had not yet been published.

Yildiz, Thuram, Locatelli, Grabara, Nico González and Ekhator are all unavailable. The expected shape is a 4-4-2. Vicario is in goal behind Kalulu, Bremer, Lucumí and Cabal. McKennie, Douglas Luiz, Koopmeiners and Alajbegovic form the midfield, with Kolo Muani and Woltemade up front.

Spalletti will skip the usual pre-match press conference. The decision was put down only to the run of closely spaced fixtures.

Fiorentina have problems of their own. Parisi, Atta and Pongračić are out, and Atta will not return until after the break. Ranieri may be fit enough for the bench. The hosts sit just above the relegation zone, but they carry a threat in Franco Mastantuono. He has had 38 shots, 11 of them on target, this Serie A season. Only Nico Paz, Kylian Mbappé and Lamine Yamal have had more in Europe’s top five leagues.

History favours the visitors. Juventus have won 82 Serie A meetings with Fiorentina, the Viola have won 37, and 55 have been drawn. Juventus have scored 275 top-flight goals against them, two fewer than Inter’s 277. A two-goal haul on Sunday would draw them level.

Kolo Muani looks the likeliest source. He has scored five of his last six Serie A goals away from home. Since February 2025, no Juventus player has more away league goals than his five, a tally that equals Dusan Vlahovic’s. He is also the only player at the club this season with at least three goals and three assists in all competitions, with four goals and three assists. He scored with Koopmeiners at AZ, taking Juventus to 11 goals after four Europa League matches.

Kerim Alajbegovic has a milestone within reach. He can become the first foreign player in Juventus’s history to score in two top-flight games in a row before turning 20.

The stakes are clear. Victory would carry Juventus into the break with three wins in a row and strengthen their bid to rejoin the European race. After it, Juventus host Venezia on 22 November at 12:30, before a trip to Como on 29 November.

#1525. GdS: Loftus-Cheek could leave Milan in January with renewal talks silent

It seems Ruben Loftus-Cheek could leave AC Milan in January, with the club hoping to invest heavily in the squad and raise the base level.

Loftus-Cheek’s Milan career is a frustrating one. He started off with a fantastic season in Serie A, but the same injury issues that had haunted him in England were present. Unfortunately, that’s the tale of his career in Italy, too.

Read SempreMilan ad-free and get access to exclusive news. Click here for a free trial!

His talent is very clearly there, but we’ve never had too much of a chance to see it on a consistent basis. It’s an unfortunate reality and this is likely to be the final full year of it.

According to Gazzetta dello Sport, as Francesco Nasato relays on X, the Rossoneri could part ways with Loftus-Cheek in the new year. There are currently no renewal talks happening, so he’ll be able to leave as a free agent in the summer.

Pre-contract discussions can begin, alternatively, someone may be a small fee to bring him to the club six months early. Either way, it seems likely that he leaves the Diavolo in 2027.

He’s currently sidelined, as the report continues, and hopes to return in late November if not early December, so time is running out for him to earn a renewal with the club. At this stage, though, it’s probably too high a mountain to climb.

An unfortunate position for everyone to be in, considering how impressive his first season was.

#1524. Spalletti skips Fiorentina preview as Juventus seek a first win over Vanoli

Luciano Spalletti will not hold his eve-of-match press conference before Sunday's trip to Fiorentina. Juventus arrive on two straight wins, chasing fourth place, against a coach Spalletti has never beaten.

Juventus will travel to Florence without the usual preview from their coach. Sunday’s game at the Franchi kicks off at 20:45. The squad got back to Turin overnight from the Netherlands. The reason given is the club’s crowded run of fixtures, TuttoJuve reported. It is the last game before the international break.

The run began with a 2-0 win over Napoli at the Allianz Stadium on 1 November. Kerim Alajbegovic scored in the 70th minute. Aged 19 years and 41 days, no foreign player had ever found the net at a younger age in a Serie A game between Juventus and Napoli.

Four days later, Juventus won 2-1 away at AZ Alkmaar in the Europa League. Teun Koopmeiners and Randal Kolo Muani scored. The result takes them to 10 points from four games in the competition. After the match, Spalletti described himself as very pleased with a solid team display against strong opponents. He felt his side should have added a third goal.

The league position still needs work. The club’s stated aim this season is fourth place, and Como currently hold that spot. The defence gives some grounds for confidence. Going back to last March, no side can match the Bianconeri’s tally of 12 shutouts. Roma are next on 11.

Vanoli and Spalletti have faced each other only twice as coaches. Both meetings were Fiorentina-Juventus fixtures last season. Last November they drew 1-1 at the Franchi. Filip Kostic gave Juventus the lead before Rolando Mandragora equalised with a long-range shot.

The hosts’ struggles on their own pitch offer Juventus an opening against a side yet to find its footing at home.

The fixture carries plenty of history. Sunday’s game is the 175th Serie A meeting between the sides, according to the club’s statistical preview. Juventus have won 82, Fiorentina 37, and 55 have ended level. Juventus have scored 275 top-flight goals against Fiorentina. Two more would draw them level with Inter’s 277, the highest total by any side against the Viola.

Once the international break is over, Juventus’s next Serie A match is on 22 November.

#1523. Bremer earns Juventus 2-2 draw at Fiorentina but leaves them six points off Champions League places

Gleison Bremer's equaliser earned Juventus a point at the Stadio Artemio Franchi after they twice fell behind against Fiorentina. Spalletti's side now go into the international break outside the Champions League places, with their next home game brought forward by a day.

The point leaves Fiorentina 15th in the table on 9 points.

The hosts led after four minutes. Mateo Pellegrino scored, set up by Pedro Goncalves. Nick Woltemade levelled in the 32nd minute from a Randal Kolo Muani assist, and it was 1-1 at half-time.

Fiorentina went ahead again in the 54th minute. Guglielmo Vicario made the first save, but the Juventus defenders were too slow to clear. Alieu Njie forced in the rebound. Bremer then reached a Douglas Luiz corner in the six-yard box before David de Gea could get to it.

Juventus completed 384 accurate passes to Fiorentina’s 273. Fiorentina still attempted 22 shots to Juventus’s 18, and both sides had 6 on target. The expected goals figures, 2.46 for Juventus and 2.14 for Fiorentina, are consistent with a fairly even contest despite the visitors’ control of the ball.

The closing stages could have gone either way. Former Juventus defender Radu Drăgușin headed in from a corner in the 82nd minute. The goal was ruled out because he pushed Bremer with both hands. Near the end, Vicario saved twice in quick succession to protect the point. Juventus also claimed a penalty when the ball struck João Mário’s arm in the Fiorentina area, but none was given.

Referee Andrea Colombo booked three Juventus players. Juan Cabal was cautioned in the 13th minute and Bremer in the 22nd. Kolo Muani was booked for dissent in the 73rd. Christ Inao Oulaï was Fiorentina’s only booking.

Juventus were without the injured Kenan Yildiz, Andrea Cambiaso, Nico González, Manuel Locatelli, Khéphren Thuram and Kamil Grabara. Weston McKennie and Zeki Çelik returned to the squad. Spalletti made three changes in the 57th minute, sending on Zhegrova for Woltemade, Alajbegovic for Boga and Celik for Cabal. Ekhator replaced McKennie in the 78th minute and Gatti came on for Lucumí in the 89th.

At his press conference at the Franchi, Spalletti said he was not happy because his team does not play at a steady enough level to aim for anything important. He did praise Kolo Muani, describing him as the player everyone wanted and one he can use as a centre-forward or out wide. Shown a replay of the João Mário incident, he dodged the question and asked, smiling, for a different one.

FT |⌛️| Termina in parità ⚪️⚫️@EASPORTSFC @easportsfcit#FiorentinaJuve pic.twitter.com/Twp629BYvj

— JuventusFC (@juventusfc) November 8, 2026

The draw ended a run of two wins, against AZ Alkmaar and Napoli. Woltemade and Pellegrino both received a rating of 8.2 from the data provider.

Next up for Juventus is Venezia, who sit 19th on 6 points. When fixture times were first set, that game was pencilled in for Monday 23 November at 20:45 Italian time.

#1522. Reports: Camarda could reunite with Abate or head abroad as Milan consider next steps

Francesco Camarda could be headed to Turin in January if AC Milan agree to a loan deal with Torino, according to new reports.

There has been plenty of discussion about where will be right for Camarda and there are several options on the table. Now, another Serie A option has emerged and they could become a priority option.

Read SempreMilan ad-free and get access to exclusive news. Click here for a free trial!

As Tuttosport (seen below) writes, understandably given their base in Turin, Torino are reportedly keen on a move for Camarda. Led by Ignazio Abate, it could be the perfect alignment for the young striker to finally regain the form which led him to the first team.

The link to Abate could be used to sweeten a deal for all parties, especially as it’s a figure the Rossoneri and Camarda trust.

However, they are not the only club with an interest; according to Gazzetta dello Sport (also seen below), the Italian striker is popular abroad. His goal against France’s U-21 side – and his general performance – have relit the market for him.

There are other clubs interested in him from Italy, but the option of a move away from the Italian system could prevail. Foreign leagues, as the report writes, ‘could capitalise on his skills and instincts as a true centre-forward’. Additionally, the lure of international experience could help him.

#1521. The molecular basis of replication fork restart via repriming by PRIMPOL

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

Eukaryotic genomes are exposed to numerous sources of DNA damage that impede replication. Only a decade ago, repriming by the primase–polymerase PRIMPOL was identified as a pathway that enables cells to tolerate DNA damage1,2,3,4. However, the molecular mechanism that underlies repriming remains poorly understood, and it is unclear how PRIMPOL is precisely targeted to stalled forks, where along single-stranded DNA PRIMPOL binds and how PRIMPOL is regulated to minimize error-prone DNA synthesis. Here, to dissect the molecular basis of repriming, we perform real-time single-molecule imaging in nuclear extracts that recapitulate genome maintenance. We directly visualize how stalled forks restart through repriming. We show that PRIMPOL is recruited to stalled forks through an interaction with the replicative helicase CDC45–MCM2–7–GINS (CMG). This facilitates primer handover from PRIMPOL to the high-fidelity polymerase ε, minimizing mutagenic DNA synthesis. At near-physiological concentrations, PRIMPOL reprimes leading strands in a CMG-dependent manner and polymerase ε extends those primers. This primary mode of repriming does not require DNA damage checkpoint signalling. PRIMPOL overexpression and checkpoint activation promote a secondary mode of repriming, whereby PRIMPOL restarts DNA synthesis far from CMG and polymerase δ extends those primers. Our data reveal a simple yet effective mechanism that directs PRIMPOL’s activity to stalled forks awaiting restart, and suggest a strategy to inhibit the repriming pathway.

Multiple pathways maintain genome stability during replication stress (RS)5, including fork reversal and translesion DNA synthesis (TLS)6. In 2013, a new RS response pathway called repriming was identified in eukaryotes1,2,3,4. PRIMPOL performs repriming and enables cells to tolerate diverse DNA lesions1,2,3,4,7,8. As it lacks proofreading, PRIMPOL has an error rate comparable to that of TLS polymerases (10−2−10−4)9,10. PRIMPOL-deficient cells and mice are hypersensitive to several DNA-damaging agents8,11,12,13, underscoring its role in genome maintenance. While repriming enables cancer cells to tolerate RS induced by oncogenes14 and chemotherapy15, PRIMPOL generates single-stranded DNA (ssDNA) gaps16,17 that sensitize cells to PARP inhibitors18,19,20. Blocking fork reversal enhances repriming, suggesting that cells favour high-fidelity pathways to minimize mutagenic DNA synthesis7,21,22.

The replicative helicase CMG unwinds parental DNA23 and is functionally coupled to polymerase ε (Pol ε)24, which synthesizes the leading strand. The lagging strand is primed and extended by primase–polymerase α (Pol α) and polymerase δ (Pol δ), respectively24. Damage on the lagging strand is readily bypassed due to the discontinuous nature of Okazaki fragment synthesis25,26. This is not the case for leading strand DNA lesions, which stall Pol ε while CMG continues to unwind DNA25,26,27. This CMG uncoupling exposes ssDNA that is rapidly coated by replication protein A (RPA)28. The notion that PRIMPOL may reprime leading strand synthesis was hypothesized at the time of its discovery2, and discussed in later work7,16,29, but there is no direct evidence for this idea.

Although repriming is a major RS response pathway and PRIMPOL is an attractive therapeutic target, key mechanistic aspects of repriming remain unclear. For example, although RPA recruits PRIMPOL to ssDNA30,31, it is unclear why PRIMPOL acts at stalled forks, but not on ssDNA generated by other processes (transcription, recombination). One study reported that high RPA concentrations inhibit PRIMPOL’s activity on ssDNA in vitro30, presumably because RPA fully coats ssDNA and prevents PRIMPOL’s access to the template. Another study found that RPA stimulated PRIMPOL’s activity on ssDNA long enough to accommodate the simultaneous binding of both proteins, that Pol ε can extend PRIMPOL’s primers in vitro and that RPA stimulates PRIMPOL’s enzymatic activity in synergy with Pol ε31. It remains unclear how repriming occurs in the nucleus, where RPA is abundant and rapidly coats exposed ssDNA. Although PRIMPOL is a known target of checkpoint kinase 1 (CHK1)22, how the DNA damage checkpoint regulates repriming remains poorly understood. Finally, it is unclear how PRIMPOL is regulated to minimize mutagenic DNA synthesis during repriming.

To address these questions, we used single-molecule imaging to directly visualize PRIMPOL-dependent fork restart in Xenopus egg extracts. We found that PRIMPOL preferentially binds near stalled forks, suggesting that it interacts with fork-associated proteins. We identified an interaction between PRIMPOL and CMG that is required for targeting PRIMPOL to stalled forks and for efficient fork restart in nuclear extract and in human cells. Our data indicate that the PRIMPOL–CMG interaction facilitates primer handover from PRIMPOL to the leading strand polymerase Pol ε, therefore minimizing mutagenic DNA synthesis. Finally, in conditions that mimic PRIMPOL overexpression, we found that PRIMPOL can reprime DNA synthesis far from the replicative helicase, and those primers are extended by Pol δ. Our findings support a simple-yet-elegant mechanism that targets PRIMPOL’s activity specifically to stalled forks and suggest a strategy to inhibit repriming.

To investigate the mechanism of PRIMPOL-dependent fork restart, we used nuclear extract prepared from Xenopus laevis eggs32. This extract contains all soluble nuclear proteins, supports efficient DNA replication and recapitulates several RS response pathways33. We could not detect frog PRIMPOL in egg extract using mass spectrometry (MS) or western blotting (Extended Data Fig. 1a,b and Supplementary Table 1). To reconstitute repriming, we supplemented nuclear extract with recombinant human PRIMPOL, which displayed robust enzymatic activity in vitro (Extended Data Fig. 1c,d).

To visualize PRIMPOL-mediated fork restart in real-time, we adapted a single-molecule assay called kinetics of eukaryotic replication via molecular imaging and tracking (KERMIT)25,34. A biotinylated linear DNA template was double-tethered onto a streptavidin-coated coverslip in a microfluidic flow-cell (Fig. 1a). DNA was incubated with high-speed supernatant—an extract that supports origin licensing but not origin firing, mimicking G1 (ref. 32) (Fig. 1a). The flow-cell was washed with buffer to remove any soluble proteins while retaining DNA-bound MCM2–7. Licensed DNA was incubated with nucleoplasmic extract—an extract that supports origin firing, elongation and RS response, mimicking S phase32 (Fig. 1a). Replication was monitored in real-time using total internal reflection fluorescence microscopy.

a, The single-molecule imaging workflow. b, Kymograms showing CMG dynamics at unperturbed forks. GINS–LD655 (orange) tracks the CMG helicase, and FEN1–KikG (blue) serves as a nascent DNA marker. c, CMG dynamics in aphidicolin-treated extract. d, CMG dynamics in Pol-α-depleted extract. e, CMG dynamics in Pol-α-depleted extract with 30 nM of WT PRIMPOL. The white arrows denote PRIMPOL-dependent fork restart events. f, Fork restart efficiency: the fraction of uncoupled CMGs that resumed fast translocation. Data are mean ± 95% confidence interval (CI) estimated by bootstrapping. n values denote the number of forks. g, CMG dynamics at DNA lesions in undepleted extract. The yellow arrows indicate fork stalling at the lesion. h, CMG speeds measured in different experiments. The blue lines indicate medians, shaded areas represent 95% CI estimated by bootstrapping. n values denote the number of CMG molecules. Ctrl, control. i, CMG dynamics at DNA lesions in extract + 30 nM of WT PRIMPOL. The white arrows indicate PRIMPOL-mediated restart events. The experiments shown in b–h were repeated twice with different extract preparations. j, Autoradiogram of plasmid replication assay in mock-depleted (i) versus Pol-α-depleted extract + buffer (ii), +3 nM WT PRIMPOL (iii), +10 nM WT PRIMPOL (iv), +30 nM WT PRIMPOL (v), +30 nM PRIMPOL(AxA) (vi) or +30 nM PRIMPOL(ΔRPA) (vii). The cartoons illustrate replication intermediates corresponding to bands on the gel (blue indicates nascent DNA). k, Quantification of the plasmid replication assay shown in j from three independent repeats. Total DNA synthesis (dark grey) or supercoiled DNA (light grey) signal was measured at 90 min and normalized to the total signal of the 30 nM WT PRIMPOL reaction. Data are mean ± s.d. from three independent experiments. P values were computed using two-sample two-sided Kolmogorov–Smirnov tests (f and h) and two-tailed two-sided Student’s t-tests (k); NS, not significant (P > 0.05); *P < 0.05, **P < 0.01, ****P < 0.0001.

To visualize CMG, we used GINS-depleted extract supplemented with fluorescently labelled GINS (GINS–LD655). To monitor DNA synthesis, we supplemented extract with FEN1–KikG (flap endonuclease 1 fused to the fluorescent protein KikG)35. FEN1 is recruited to chromatin through its interaction with PCNA36, and was previously validated as a marker of nascent DNA37, which does not require FEN1’s enzymatic activity37.

In mock-depleted extract, origin firing generated two diverging CMGs travelling at around 300 nucleotides per min with FEN1–KikG signal accumulating behind each helicase (Fig. 1b). To induce RS, the extract was supplemented with 15 µM aphidicolin (APH)—an inhibitor of B-family polymerases (including α, ε and δ) that does not inhibit PRIMPOL (Extended Data Fig. 1d). In APH-treated extract, CMG travelled around 10× slower than in mock without any accompanying FEN1–KikG signal, indicating a failure to synthesize DNA (Fig. 1c). This substantial CMG slowing during RS (reported by us25 and others38) is a hallmark of CMG uncoupling28 (Fig. 1b,c). Adding 30 nM of wild-type (WT) PRIMPOL to APH-treated extract did not support fork restart (Extended Data Fig. 1e), reflecting the fact that APH inhibits Pol ε and δ and prevents them from extending PRIMPOL’s primers.

To recapitulate RS without inhibiting Pol ε/δ, we devised two independent strategies. First, we immunodepleted Pol α from nuclear extract (depleting or inhibiting Pol α was previously used to induce RS in cells22,39,40,41). In Pol-α-depleted extract, CMGs travelled very slowly (around 30 nucleotides per min) without any accompanying FEN1 accumulation (Fig. 1d). This is indicative of helicase uncoupling and is consistent with reports that Pol α is required for establishing leading strand synthesis42,43. When Pol-α-depleted extract was supplemented with recombinant WT PRIMPOL, we routinely observed that slow/uncoupled CMGs suddenly sped up to around 300 nucleotides per min (Fig. 1e (white arrows)). We interpret this switch to fast CMG progression as fork restart. Around 75% of stalled forks restarted in Pol-α-depleted extract supplemented with 30 nM WT PRIMPOL, versus only around 5% restart efficiency in reactions supplemented with buffer (Fig. 1f and Extended Data Fig. 1f). Importantly, the sudden switch from slow to fast CMG progression was accompanied by FEN1–KikG accumulation behind the fork, indicative of DNA synthesis (Fig. 1e). To corroborate the idea that fast CMG progression corresponds to DNA synthesis, we repeated these experiments with fluorescently labelled PCNA (PCNA–LD655)—an established marker of nascent DNA44,45. Like FEN1–KikG, PCNA–LD655 accumulated behind restarted forks (Extended Data Fig. 1g). Disrupting FEN1’s interaction with PCNA eliminated FEN1–KikG binding (Extended Data Fig. 1h) without impacting fork restart (Extended Data Fig. 1i). We conclude that FEN1–KikG is recruited to nascent DNA by PCNA, and that the sudden speed-up of CMG represents fork restart. We subsequently used FEN1–KikG as a DNA synthesis marker because it provided better signal-to-noise than PCNA–LD655 (Methods).

Second, we designed a DNA substrate with site-specific DNA lesions on the leading strand template, each consisting of a small (around 4 amino acids) peptide adduct (Extended Data Fig. 2a). This lesion should easily fit through CMG’s central channel46, and should induce helicase uncoupling. After encountering the lesion, CMG instantly slowed down from around 300 nucleotides per min to 30 nucleotides per min (Fig. 1g,h), indicative of uncoupling. In the absence of PRIMPOL, forks stalled at the lesion restarted very inefficiently (around 7%) (Fig. 1f and Extended Data Fig. 1f), probably through TLS as shown previously47,48. In extract containing 30 nM of WT PRIMPOL, around 50% of forks stalled at the lesion restarted (Fig. 1i,f), causing CMG to speed up from around 30 nucleotides per min to 300 nucleotides per min—matching the speed of unperturbed forks (Fig. 1h and Extended Data Fig. 2b). Importantly, lesion-stalled forks restarted in a PRIMPOL-dependent manner in extract containing endogenous levels of Pol α.

We conclude that recombinant human WT PRIMPOL supports robust fork restart in our single-molecule assay using two orthogonal sources of RS (Fig. 1f). We subsequently used the Pol α depletion method because it provided a higher throughput, and was easily adapted for ensemble assays (see below).

To establish an ensemble assay for PRIMPOL-dependent fork restart, we replicated a 3 kb plasmid in Pol-α-depleted extract, which strongly suppressed DNA synthesis in comparison to the mock-depleted extract (Fig. 1j (compare i and ii)). The low levels of DNA synthesis in Pol-α-depleted extract (Fig. 1j (ii)) are probably caused by trace amounts of Pol α that evaded the immunodepletion (Extended Data Fig. 2c).

Supplementing Pol-α-depleted extract with 3–30 nM of WT PRIMPOL led to a significant increase in DNA synthesis, in a PRIMPOL-concentration-dependent manner (Fig. 1j,k). As human cells contain around 17 nM of PRIMPOL49, the concentrations used here are near physiological. Notably, 30 nM of WT PRIMPOL did not fully rescue DNA synthesis (Fig. 1j (v versus i)). We attribute this to the fact that depleting Pol α activates the DNA damage checkpoint (Extended Data Fig. 2c), which partially inhibits origin firing and results in fewer forks (Extended Data Fig. 2d (CDC45 blot)). We revisit CHK1’s role in Fig. 4.

To verify that PRIMPOL is responsible for the partial rescue of DNA synthesis in the biochemical assay, we tested two previously characterized mutants: (1) PRIMPOL D114A/E116A (hereafter, PRIMPOL(AxA)), which lacks primase and polymerase activity2,3; and (2) PRIMPOL D519R/F522A/D551R/I554A (hereafter, PRIMPOL(ΔRPA)), which cannot interact with RPA30 (Extended Data Fig. 1c). The in vitro primase–polymerase assay showed that PRIMPOL(ΔRPA) (but not PRIMPOL(AxA)) exhibits catalytic activity (Extended Data Fig. 1d). Chromatin fractionation experiments indicate that WT PRIMPOL and PRIMPOL(AxA) (but not PRIMPOL(ΔRPA)) are recruited to DNA in Pol-α-depleted extract (Extended Data Fig. 2d) and in APH-treated extract (Extended Data Fig. 2e). In contrast to WT PRIMPOL, neither PRIMPOL(AxA) nor PRIMPOL(ΔRPA) rescued DNA synthesis in Pol-α-depleted extract (Fig. 1j (v–vii)), corroborating reports that repriming requires both PRIMPOL’s enzymatic activity1,4 and its interaction with RPA30,31. These data indicate that Pol-α-depleted extract recapitulates PRIMPOL-dependent fork restart, providing a powerful model system to dissect the molecular mechanism of repriming.

It was previously proposed that RPA recruits PRIMPOL to stalled forks4,30. As uncoupled CMGs generate long tracts of RPA-coated ssDNA, it remained unclear where exactly PRIMPOL binds along ssDNA. To address this question, we visualized AlexaFluor647-labelled WT PRIMPOL (PRIMPOL(WT)–AF647) in Pol-α-depleted extract supplemented with FEN1–KikG, and RPA fused to mCherry-XL50,51 (hereafter, RPA–mCherryXL) (Extended Data Fig. 3a). This enabled us to simultaneously monitor PRIMPOL binding and dissociation, DNA synthesis and the extent of RPA–ssDNA. Importantly, fluorescent labelling did not impair PRIMPOL’s fork restart activity (Extended Data Fig. 3b,c).

At 30 nM of PRIMPOL(WT)–AF647, there were too many PRIMPOL binding events on RPA–ssDNA, making it impossible to resolve individual molecules (Extended Data Fig. 3d). To distinguish each PRIMPOL binding event, we visualized 3 nM PRIMPOL(WT)–AF647 at 15 s per frame (Fig. 2a). Initially, RPA–ssDNA tracts grew bidirectionally very slowly (Fig. 2a and Extended Data Fig. 3e)—consistent with uncoupled helicases (Fig. 1h). After PRIMPOL-mediated fork restart, RPA–ssDNA tracts grew rapidly, but the RPA signal intensity decreased around twofold (Fig. 2a (bottom)). This suggests that PRIMPOL reprimes synthesis only on one strand (the leading strand, as shown in Fig. 4).

a, Kymogram showing ssDNA coated with RPA–mCherryXL (green) and nascent DNA coated with FEN1–KikG (blue) in Pol-α-depleted extract with 3 nM PRIMPOL(WT)–AF647 (magenta). For clarity, the RPA kymogram is shown separately from FEN1 + PRIMPOL. The grey lines mark the boundary of the RPA signal: the dotted lines denote uncoupled CMGs and the dashed lines mark restarted forks. The white arrows indicate fork restart. Bottom inset: integrated RPA signal profile, which decreases by around 50% after fork restart. b, RPA–mCherryXL (green), FEN1–KikG (blue) and PRIMPOL(WT)–AF647 (magenta) binding to DNA in Pol-α-depleted extract. The cartoons illustrate the fork status over time. c, Cumulative probability plot of PRIMPOL(WT)–AF647 (3 nM) binding event duration, comparing fork-proximal (dark grey) and fork-distal (light grey) binding events in Pol-α-depleted extract (solid lines) or APH-treated extract (dashed lines). n values denote the number of binding events analysed. d, The number of all fork-proximal PRIMPOL binding events per unit time at the fork. e, The number of fork-distal PRIMPOL binding events observed per unit time normalized by the length of exposed ssDNA. In d and e, n values denote the number of forks. Data are mean ± 95% CI, estimated by bootstrapping. f, Cumulative probability plot of fork-proximal (solid lines) and fork-distal (dashed lines) binding events in Pol-α-depleted extract for PRIMPOL(WT)–AF647 (dark grey) and PRIMPOL(AxA)–AF647 (orange). n values denote the number of binding events analysed. Data in a–f are from experiments imaged at 15 s per frame. g, Kymograms showing fork restart in Pol-α-depleted extract with 3 nM PRIMPOL(WT)–AF647 (magenta) imaged at 3 s per frame. h, Cumulative probability plot of PRIMPOL(WT)–AF647 binding event duration in Pol-α-depleted extract imaged at 3 s per frame (at this temporal resolution, short-lived events dominate both fork-distal and fork-proximal subpopulations). n values denote the number of binding events analysed. P values were computed using two-sample two-sided Kolmogorov–Smirnov tests (c–f and h); ***P < 0.001. All experiments were performed twice, with different extract preparations.

We detected numerous short-lived PRIMPOL(WT)–AF647 binding events far from replication forks (Fig. 2a (orange triangles)), which we call fork-distal. Most fork-distal PRIMPOL binding events (~84%) lasted one frame (15 s) or less (Fig. 2c) and were randomly distributed along RPA–ssDNA. We also detected fork-proximal PRIMPOL binding events close to the fork (within 1 pixel = 160 nm), which tended to be longer than fork-distal binding events (Fig. 2c). Notably, long-lived fork-proximal PRIMPOL(WT)–AF647 binding (Fig. 2a,b (curly brackets)) preceded most (~70 ± 10%) fork restart events (Fig. 2a,b (white arrows)).

To gain further insights, we quantified the frequency of fork-proximal (Fig. 2d) and fork-distal (Fig. 2e) binding events in Pol-α-depleted extract supplemented with 3 nM of fluorescently labelled WT PRIMPOL, PRIMPOL(AxA) or PRIMPOL(ΔRPA). As expected, PRIMPOL(ΔRPA) exhibited very little fork-proximal or fork-distal binding in Pol-α-depleted extract, indistinguishable from the negative control, for which we measured the frequency of non-specific binding using free AF647 dye (Fig. 2d,e and Extended Data Fig. 3f). Both WT PRIMPOL and PRIMPOL(AxA) exhibited high levels of fork-proximal and fork-distal binding in Pol-α-depleted extract, consistent with chromatin fractionation experiments (Extended Data Fig. 2d,e). Notably, PRIMPOL(AxA) exhibited the most fork-proximal binding (Fig. 2d), probably because it can repeatedly bind to stalled forks without restarting them (Extended Data Fig. 3g). By contrast, WT PRIMPOL promotes fork restart, after which it no longer binds to the unstressed fork (the mock-depleted control is shown in Fig. 2d and Extended Data Fig. 3h). Notably, there was no statistical difference between binding event durations for WT PRIMPOL and PRIMPOL(AxA) (Fig. 2f), even though only WT PRIMPOL supported fork restart (Extended Data Fig. 2i).

We also observed long-lived fork-proximal WT PRIMPOL binding events before fork restart on the template with a site-specific lesion (Extended Data Fig. 3j). These productive WT PRIMPOL binding events lasted around 3 min, similar to those measured in Pol-α-depleted extract (Extended Data Fig. 3j). Notably, there was a delay of 3–5 min between the dissociation of PRIMPOL(WT)–AF647 from the fork, and fork restart (Extended Data Fig. 3j). This delay probably reflects the time needed for a replicative polymerase to capture the primer synthesized by PRIMPOL, and for the reassembly of an active replisome.

Occasionally, we observed PRIMPOL binding in consecutive movie frames at nearby positions on DNA (Fig. 2b (light blue ovals)). This could represent a PRIMPOL molecule diffusing along ssDNA, or may represent different molecules binding at slightly different positions along ssDNA. To distinguish between these scenarios, we repeated the experiment at 3 s per frame (Fig. 2g, five times faster than in Fig. 2a–f). At this higher frame rate, we frequently observed different PRIMPOL molecules briefly binding to ssDNA in non-consecutive video frames (Fig. 2g (white ovals)). Such binding sequences could be misinterpreted as diffusion of a single PRIMPOL molecule if imaged at lower framerates. This experiment also revealed that the vast majority of PRIMPOL binding events are very short-lived, lasting 3 s or less (Fig. 2h). We still observed long-lived fork-proximal binding events that preceded fork restart (Fig. 2g (white curly brackets)). In summary, although we cannot rule out PRIMPOL diffusion across short distances, our data argue against long-range PRIMPOL diffusion on ssDNA.

Although PRIMPOL can transiently bind anywhere along ssDNA–RPA (Fig. 2a,b), the vast majority (over 99%) of binding events are non-productive—that is, they do not lead to fork restart. Productive PRIMPOL binding events occur predominantly near stalled forks and tend to be long-lived (~3 min; Extended Data Fig. 3j), raising the question of why fork-proximal binding events are longer. We hypothesized that PRIMPOL’s binding at the fork may be stabilized by yet unknown interactions with fork-associated proteins. Notably, AlphaFold3 predicted that several replisome subunits may interact with PRIMPOL52. By cross-referencing AlphaFold predictions for human and frog proteins, we singled out PRIMPOL’s putative interaction with MCM4—a CMG subunit (Fig. 3a). Positively charged residues in human PRIMPOL (Arg29, Arg31, Lys34) are predicted to form salt bridges with MCM4 residues (Fig. 3a and Extended Data Fig. 4a,b). To test this prediction, we generated three mutants: PRIMPOL R29A/R31A/K34A (hereafter, PRIMPOL(3A)), PRIMPOL R29D/R31E/K34D (hereafter, PRIMPOL(DED)) and PRIMPOL(29–35:Linker) (in which residues 29–35 were replaced with the linker GGGSGGGS) (Fig. 3b and Extended Data Fig. 4c,d).
